meanings.short: A quantity with components labelled by indices that change by a fixed rule when coordinates change, so the object itself stays the same.
meanings.long: Numbers (scalars) and vectors are the simplest tensors. A tensor of type (m, n) takes n vectors and m one-forms and returns a number, linearly in each; the metric is a (0, 2) tensor. Because tensors change in step with coordinates, an equation between tensors that holds in one frame holds in all.

meanings.short: A linear rule that takes a vector and returns a number, written with a lower index; the partner of a vector.
meanings.long: A one-form is a (0, 1) tensor. The gradient of a function is the standard example: fed a displacement, it gives the change in the function. The metric turns each vector into a one-form and back, by lowering or raising its index.

meanings.short: The one-form made from the partial derivatives of a function, which gives the function's change along any displacement it is fed.
meanings.long: Its components are ∂φ/∂xᵅ, with lower indices. It is the spacetime version of the familiar gradient ∇φ.

everyday: In everyday speech manifold means many and various, or a set of pipes in an engine; in maths it is a kind of space.

meanings.short: A space that looks like ordinary flat space close up around each point but may be curved or connected up differently on large scales.
meanings.long: The surface of a sphere is a two-dimensional manifold: each small patch looks like a flat plane. In general relativity spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold with a metric.

meanings.short: The four-vector tangent to a body's world line, its rate of change of position in spacetime per unit of its own proper time.
meanings.long: Its components are dxᵅ/dτ. Its squared length is always the same, minus one in units with c = 1 and the signature (−, +, +, +), and in the body's own rest frame it points purely along time.

meanings.short: The four-vector that combines a body's energy and its ordinary momentum; for a massive body, mass times four-velocity.
meanings.long: Its time component is the energy and its space components the momentum, as measured by a given observer. Its length gives the rest mass, the same for every observer. Light has a four-momentum of zero length.

meanings.short: The rate of change of a body's four-velocity per unit of proper time, always at right angles to the four-velocity in spacetime.
meanings.long: A freely falling body has zero four-acceleration. Its length is the acceleration the body itself would feel and measure.

meanings.short: A set of basis vectors, each along one coordinate direction, sized so that a small coordinate change maps straight onto a displacement.
meanings.long: In spherical coordinates the coordinate basis vector along θ has length r, not 1, unlike the unit vector of an orthonormal basis. The metric's components in a coordinate basis are the dot products of the basis vectors.

meanings.short: A set of basis vectors that are all at right angles to each other and all of length one.
meanings.long: Components in an orthonormal basis are found simply by taking dot products. In relativity an observer's orthonormal basis is one time direction and three space directions, with the metric taking its plain Minkowski form.

meanings.short: The matrix inverse of the metric, written with upper indices, used to raise indices and turn one-forms into vectors.
meanings.long: Multiplied by the metric it gives the identity, the Kronecker delta. For a diagonal metric its entries are simply one over the metric's entries.

meanings.short: Using the metric to turn an upper index into a lower one, or the inverse metric to turn a lower one into an upper one.
meanings.long: Lowering the index of a vector with the metric gives the matching one-form, whose components are the metric times the vector, summed over the repeated index. Because the metric's covariant derivative is zero, it can be moved freely through derivatives while doing this.

meanings.short: An index that appears once in each term of an equation and is not summed, so the equation holds for each of its values.
meanings.long: Every term of a valid equation must have the same free indices, in the same up or down positions. That is a quick check on any calculation.

meanings.short: An index that appears twice in one term, usually once up and once down, and is summed over, so it can be renamed freely.
meanings.long: In the sum of A with an upper α times B with a lower α, the index α is a dummy index: the result is a single number and means the same if α is renamed β.

meanings.short: Setting an upper and a lower index of a tensor equal and summing over them, which removes both and gives a tensor of lower rank.
meanings.long: Contracting a vector with a one-form gives a number; contracting the Riemann tensor gives the Ricci tensor, and contracting that gives the Ricci scalar. For a matrix, contraction is the trace.

everyday: In everyday speech a contraction is a shrinking; here it is an operation on indices.

meanings.short: Making something symmetric under swapping some of its parts, such as two indices of a tensor or two identical particles, by averaging over every order.
meanings.long: For two indices, T(αβ) = ½(Tαβ + Tβα), written with round brackets round the indices.

meanings.short: Making something change sign whenever two chosen parts are swapped, such as two tensor indices or two identical fermions, by averaging with signs.
meanings.long: For two indices, T[αβ] = ½(Tαβ − Tβα), written with square brackets round the indices. The result is zero if the tensor was symmetric in those indices.

meanings.short: The frame in which the total ordinary momentum of a group of particles is zero, the natural frame for a collision.
meanings.long: In relativity it replaces the centre-of-mass frame. The total energy measured there is the invariant mass of the system, which sets, for example, the threshold for making new particles.

meanings.short: A tensor that records the density and flow of energy and momentum at each point of spacetime: the source of gravity in general relativity.
meanings.long: Its time-time component is the energy density, its time-space components the energy flux and momentum density, and its space-space part the pressures and stresses. Conservation of energy and momentum says its divergence is zero. The Einstein field equations set it proportional to the Einstein tensor.

meanings.short: A fluid fully described by its density and pressure in its own rest frame, with no viscosity, heat flow or other stresses.
meanings.long: Its stress-energy tensor is (ρ + P) times the four-velocity twice, plus P times the metric. Stars, dust and the cosmic matter and radiation of cosmology are all modelled as perfect fluids.

meanings.short: A rule linking a system's state variables, such as pressure, density or volume, and temperature; for an ideal gas, PV = NkT.
meanings.long: In cosmology it is often written P = wρc², with w = 0 for matter, 1/3 for radiation and −1 for vacuum energy. For a star it decides how much mass pressure can hold up.

meanings.short: A small region of spacetime around a freely falling observer, with coordinates in which the laws of special relativity hold.
meanings.long: There the metric is the flat Minkowski metric and its first derivatives vanish at the chosen point; gravity shows up only through second derivatives, as tides. It is how general relativity builds on special relativity.

meanings.short: The frame of an observer moving under gravity alone, in which gravity cannot be felt nearby.
meanings.long: By the equivalence principle a freely falling laboratory behaves, over a small region, like one floating far from all masses. Only tidal effects across a large region give gravity away.

meanings.short: The principle that in a small enough region of spacetime all the laws of physics, not just motion, take their special-relativity form.
meanings.long: It goes beyond the weak equivalence principle, which is only about how bodies fall. Names differ between textbooks; 8.962 follows Carroll's usage.

meanings.short: The recipe for moving a law from flat to curved spacetime: replace the flat metric by the general metric and ordinary derivatives by covariant ones.
meanings.long: It adds no new coupling to curvature beyond what the equivalence principle demands. It is not a theorem but a guess, judged by experiment; so far it has passed every test.

meanings.short: A derivative suited to curved space or curved coordinates that corrects for the basis vectors changing from place to place, so it gives a tensor.
meanings.long: For a vector it is the partial derivative plus Christoffel-symbol terms. It reduces to the ordinary derivative in a local Lorentz frame, and the covariant derivative of the metric is zero.

meanings.short: A derivative with an extra term for the vector potential, so that equations keep their form when the gauge is changed.
meanings.long: It is (ħ/i)∇ − (q/c)A acting on a wavefunction. Under a gauge change it changes only by the same phase factor as the wavefunction itself.

meanings.short: The rule that says how to compare vectors at neighbouring points of a curved space, and so defines the covariant derivative.
meanings.long: Its components are the Christoffel symbols. Many connections are possible in principle; general relativity uses the one that is torsion-free and metric compatible, which is fixed by the metric.

everyday: In everyday speech a connection is any link; here it is a precise rule of geometry.

meanings.short: Of a connection: its covariant derivative of the metric is zero, so parallel transport keeps lengths and angles unchanged.
meanings.long: Together with being torsion-free this fixes the connection uniquely: its components are the Christoffel symbols built from the metric.

meanings.short: An object that changes like a tensor under a change of coordinates except for an extra power of the Jacobian determinant.
meanings.long: That power is its weight. The determinant of the metric is a density of weight −2, so multiplying a density by a suitable power of √|g| turns it into a true tensor. The volume element √−g d⁴x is the main use.

meanings.short: A symbol with one index per dimension: +1 for an even order of the indices, −1 for an odd order, 0 if any repeat.
meanings.long: In three dimensions it writes the cross product and the determinant compactly. In curved spacetime it is a tensor density of weight 1, not a tensor.

meanings.short: The Levi-Civita symbol multiplied by the square root of the size of the metric's determinant, which makes it a true tensor.
meanings.long: It is used to build volumes and dual tensors in curved spacetime in a way that does not depend on the coordinates.

meanings.short: Carrying a vector along a curve while keeping it as unchanged as the curved space allows, so its covariant derivative along the curve is zero.
meanings.long: In flat space it simply keeps the vector pointing the same way. In curved space the result depends on the path, and a vector carried round a closed loop comes back turned, which measures curvature. A geodesic parallel transports its own tangent vector.

meanings.short: A way of labelling points along a geodesic so that the geodesic equation takes its simple form; proper time is one, for bodies with mass.
meanings.long: Any other affine parameter is a constant multiple of it plus a constant. For light, which has no proper time, an affine parameter takes its place.

meanings.short: The rate of change of a tensor as it is dragged along the flow of a vector field, compared with the tensor already there.
meanings.long: It needs no metric or connection, only the vector field. A Killing vector is one along which the Lie derivative of the metric vanishes, so moving along it leaves the geometry unchanged.

everyday: Named after the mathematician Wilhelm Killing; it has nothing to do with killing.

meanings.short: A direction of symmetry of a spacetime: a vector field along which the geometry does not change.
meanings.long: If the metric does not depend on some coordinate, the basis vector along it is a Killing vector. Each Killing vector gives a quantity conserved along every geodesic, such as energy for a static spacetime or angular momentum for a round one.

meanings.short: The condition that a vector field is a Killing vector: the symmetrised covariant derivative of its lowered form is zero.
meanings.long: It says the symmetrised covariant derivative of the Killing vector, with its index lowered, vanishes. It is the coordinate-free way of saying that the Lie derivative of the metric along the vector is zero.

meanings.short: A symmetric tensor with two or more indices that, fed a geodesic's momentum, gives a conserved number, like a Killing vector does with one index.
meanings.long: It expresses a hidden symmetry that no Killing vector captures. In an expanding FRW universe one gives the redshift of light; in the Kerr spacetime one gives the Carter constant.

meanings.short: The tensor that measures the curvature of a space or spacetime: how much a vector turns when carried round a small closed loop.
meanings.long: It is built from the Christoffel symbols and their derivatives and has four indices. It vanishes everywhere exactly when the space is flat. Its physical meaning in gravity is tides: it sets how neighbouring freely falling bodies accelerate apart or together.

origin: Greek holos, whole, and nomos, law.

meanings.short: The turning of a vector that has been parallel transported round a closed loop, a sign of curvature inside the loop.
meanings.long: On a sphere a vector carried round a triangle comes back turned by an angle equal to the triangle's area divided by the radius squared. In flat space there is no holonomy.

meanings.short: A symmetric two-index tensor made by contracting the Riemann tensor: the part of curvature that changes volumes.
meanings.long: It is the Riemann tensor contracted on its first and third indices. In vacuum the Einstein equations say it vanishes, though the Riemann tensor need not, which is how tides and gravitational waves exist in empty space.

meanings.short: A single number at each point that sums up curvature: the Ricci tensor contracted with the metric.
meanings.long: For a sphere of radius a it is 2/a². It is the Lagrangian density of the Einstein–Hilbert action.

meanings.short: The curvature tensor on the left of Einstein's field equations: the Ricci tensor minus half the metric times the Ricci scalar.
meanings.long: By the Bianchi identity its divergence is always zero, which matches the conservation of energy and momentum in the stress-energy tensor it is set equal to (times 8πG).

meanings.short: The part of the Riemann tensor left after removing its Ricci parts: the curvature that can exist in empty space.
meanings.long: In four dimensions the Riemann tensor has 20 independent components, 10 in the Ricci tensor and 10 in the Weyl tensor. Gravitational waves and tides in vacuum are carried by the Weyl tensor.

meanings.short: A rule that the covariant derivatives of the Riemann tensor, summed over cyclic orders of three indices, always add to zero.
meanings.long: Contracted twice, it shows that the Einstein tensor has zero divergence. That is why the Einstein equations are consistent with the conservation of energy and momentum.

meanings.short: The way two neighbouring geodesics drift apart or together because of curvature, the relativistic description of tides.
meanings.long: The relative acceleration of the separation vector between two nearby freely falling bodies is set by the Riemann tensor. In flat spacetime it is zero.

meanings.short: Of a two-index tensor in four dimensions: changed by subtracting half the metric times its trace, which flips the sign of the trace.
meanings.long: The Einstein tensor is the trace-reversed Ricci tensor. In linearised gravity the trace-reversed metric perturbation makes the field equations simpler.

meanings.short: Coordinates built round one event so that spacetime looks flat there: the metric is Minkowski and its first derivatives vanish.
meanings.long: The second derivatives of the metric cannot all be removed; what is left is the Riemann tensor.

meanings.short: Coordinates built along a whole freely falling world line, rather than at one event, so that spacetime looks flat all along it.
meanings.long: They describe what a freely falling observer measures nearby: only tidal effects of curvature remain.

meanings.short: The action of general relativity: the Ricci scalar added up over spacetime, whose variation gives Einstein's field equations.
meanings.long: It is S = (1/16πG) ∫ R √−g d⁴x. Adding the action of matter and varying the metric gives the full field equations with the stress-energy tensor as source. Hilbert presented it in November 1915, at almost the same time as Einstein's final field equations, and credited Einstein with the physical ideas.

meanings.short: A way of deriving Einstein's equations by varying the metric and the connection of the action independently.
meanings.long: Varying the metric gives the field equations; varying the connection forces it to be metric compatible, so the usual connection comes out of the action instead of being assumed.

meanings.short: A theory of gravity that adds a scalar field to the metric, so that the strength of gravity can vary from place to place.
meanings.long: Brans–Dicke theory is the best-known example. Solar-system tests and gravitational waves limit how much they can differ from general relativity.

meanings.short: The relativistic wave equation for a field without spin: the ordinary wave equation with an extra term for the particle's mass.
meanings.long: With zero mass it is the ordinary wave equation. It follows from the simplest Lagrangian for a scalar field.

meanings.short: Of a spacetime: becoming flat, like special relativity's, far away from all the matter in it.
meanings.long: The spacetime round an isolated star or black hole is asymptotically flat, so far-away observers can use it to define the total mass and time. An expanding universe is not.

meanings.short: The solution of Einstein's equations for the empty spacetime outside a round, non-spinning, uncharged mass.
meanings.long: Karl Schwarzschild found it in 1915 and published it early in 1916. It describes the gravity outside the Sun and outside any non-spinning star, and, extended inwards past r = 2GM/c², a black hole.

meanings.short: The usual coordinates t, r, θ, φ for a round spacetime, with r chosen so that a sphere of radius r has area 4πr².
meanings.long: t is the time kept by distant observers. They behave badly at the horizon, r = 2GM/c², though spacetime itself is fine there.

meanings.short: Coordinates for a round spacetime whose space part is the flat metric times one factor, the same in every direction.
meanings.long: Unlike Schwarzschild coordinates, they treat radial and sideways distances alike, which is convenient for some calculations and for comparing with Newtonian gravity.

meanings.short: A radius defined by area: the r for which a sphere around the centre has area 4πr², whatever the true distance to the centre.
meanings.long: In curved space the distance to the centre need not equal r. The Schwarzschild r is an areal radius.

meanings.short: The result that the empty spacetime outside any round distribution of matter is the Schwarzschild spacetime, even if the matter moves.
meanings.long: So a star that pulsates while staying round sends out no gravitational waves, and the outside of a round star depends only on its total mass.

meanings.short: The result that, in a round distribution of matter, the motion at any radius depends only on the mass inside that radius.
meanings.long: Matter outside a sphere has no effect inside it; this is the inside half of Birkhoff's theorem, which Newtonian cosmology relies on.

meanings.short: The equations of general relativity for a static, round star of fluid: hydrostatic equilibrium with gravity made stronger by pressure.
meanings.long: Given an equation of state, they are integrated outwards from the centre until the pressure falls to zero, which gives the star's radius and mass. They set the maximum mass of a neutron star.

meanings.short: In a round star, the mass inside areal radius r, defined from the metric; outside the star it equals the total mass.
meanings.long: It obeys dm/dr = 4πr²ρ, the same equation as in Newtonian gravity, though the volume element is not 4πr² dr in curved space.

meanings.short: A simple model equation of state in which pressure is a fixed power Γ of density, P = Kρ to the power Γ.
meanings.long: Real matter is more complicated, but polytropes are easy to work with and capture the main behaviour, so they are used for tests and teaching.

meanings.short: The result that a static round star of fluid must have a radius larger than 9/4 times GM/c², or its central pressure would be infinite.
meanings.long: Anything more compact must collapse. It holds under mild assumptions, such as density not increasing outwards.

meanings.short: A number made by contracting the Riemann tensor with itself, used to test whether curvature is really infinite somewhere.
meanings.long: For Schwarzschild it is 48G²M²/r⁶ (units with c = 1): finite at the horizon r = 2GM/c², so that is a coordinate singularity, but infinite at r = 0, a true singularity.

meanings.short: A place where a metric's components blow up or vanish only because of a poor choice of coordinates, not because spacetime is singular.
meanings.long: The Schwarzschild horizon is one: curvature invariants are finite there, and coordinates such as Kruskal's or Eddington–Finkelstein's pass through it smoothly.

meanings.short: A region of spacetime from which nothing, not even light, can escape, formed when matter collapses beyond its own horizon.
meanings.long: Its boundary is the event horizon; for a non-spinning black hole of mass M its radius is 2GM/c². By the no-hair theorem a settled black hole is described by its mass, spin and charge alone.

meanings.short: The surface round a black hole from inside which no signal can ever get out to the rest of the universe.
meanings.long: For a non-spinning black hole it lies at the Schwarzschild radius, 2GM/c². Light emitted just outside it reaches far-away observers ever more redshifted; at the horizon the redshift becomes infinite.

meanings.short: The collapsed core of a massive star, about 20 km across but more massive than the Sun, made mostly of neutrons.
meanings.long: It is held up by the pressure of neutrons squeezed together, and has a maximum mass of about two to three Suns, above which it must become a black hole. Spinning neutron stars are seen as pulsars.

meanings.short: A radial coordinate for a black hole chosen so that light moving inwards or outwards travels one unit of it per unit of time.
meanings.long: It stretches the region near the horizon to minus infinity, so a light ray seems to take forever to get there, like the tortoise of Zeno's paradox.

meanings.short: Coordinates for a black hole built from light rays, in which falling objects pass smoothly through the horizon.
meanings.long: The ingoing version uses v = t + r* in place of t. Its light cones tip over smoothly as r falls, showing that inside the horizon everything moves inwards.

meanings.short: A map of a whole spacetime squeezed onto a finite page, with light rays still at 45 degrees, to show its causal structure.
meanings.long: Infinity is brought to a finite edge by a change of coordinates that keeps angles of light cones. It shows at a glance which regions can send signals to which.

meanings.short: The solution of Einstein's equations for a spinning black hole, found by Roy Kerr in 1963.
meanings.long: It depends on the mass and the spin. Near the hole space is dragged round with the spin, so orbits going with it and against it differ.

meanings.short: The solution for a black hole that both spins and carries electric charge, the most general settled black hole.
meanings.long: With zero charge it becomes the Kerr metric, with zero spin the Reissner–Nordström metric, and with neither the Schwarzschild metric.

meanings.short: The solution of Einstein's equations for a round, non-spinning black hole with electric charge.
meanings.long: It has two horizons when the charge is smaller than the mass (in suitable units), and none, a naked singularity, when the charge is larger.

meanings.short: A singularity of infinite curvature not hidden behind an event horizon, so it could be seen from outside.
meanings.long: Solutions with too much charge or spin for their mass have one. Penrose's cosmic censorship idea, unproven, says nature never forms them from ordinary collapse.

meanings.short: The result that a settled black hole is completely described by three numbers: its mass, spin and electric charge.
meanings.long: Any other feature of what fell in, its shape or what it was made of, is radiated away or swallowed. The name is a joke: black holes have no hair.

meanings.short: The half-joking name for the rule that a newly formed black hole radiates away every feature it can, leaving only mass, spin and charge.
meanings.long: It comes from Richard Price's early calculations of how distorted black holes settle down by giving off gravitational waves.

meanings.short: The twisting of spacetime near a spinning mass, which drags nearby gyroscopes and orbits round with the spin.
meanings.long: It is tiny near the Earth, but was measured by the Gravity Probe B satellite. Near a spinning black hole it is strong enough that nothing can stay still.

meanings.short: The part of weak gravity produced by moving or spinning masses, which acts on moving bodies much as a magnetic field acts on charges.
meanings.long: In linearised gravity the metric splits into a Newtonian, gravitoelectric part and a gravitomagnetic part from mass currents. Frame dragging is its best-known effect.

meanings.short: Of the part of weak gravity that comes from mass at rest: ordinary Newtonian gravity, which resembles the electric field of a charge.
meanings.long: It is set by the Newtonian potential. Moving masses add a gravitomagnetic part.

meanings.short: The circular orbit, at 1.5 times the horizon radius of a non-spinning black hole, where light can circle the hole, though unstably.
meanings.long: Light nudged off it either falls in or escapes after several turns. Seen from afar it makes a bright thin ring round the black hole's shadow, which the Event Horizon Telescope imaged.

meanings.short: The smallest circular orbit round a black hole in which a body can stay without spiralling in: for a non-spinning hole, three horizon radii.
meanings.long: Closer in, the effective potential has no minimum, so a small nudge sends the body plunging. It marks the inner edge of the discs of gas round black holes.

meanings.short: A network of radio telescopes across the Earth that work together as one Earth-sized dish to image the regions around black holes.
meanings.long: In 2019 it published the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87; in 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. Both came after Guth's 2013 lectures in 8.286.

meanings.short: General relativity for weak gravity: spacetime is treated as flat plus a small change to the metric, and only first-order terms are kept.
meanings.long: The equations become linear, so solutions can be added. It gives Newtonian gravity, gravitomagnetism and gravitational waves.

meanings.short: The case of weak gravity and slow motion, in which general relativity must reduce to Newton's law of gravity.
meanings.long: Matching the two fixes the constant in Einstein's equations as 8πG. The time-time part of the metric then gives the Newtonian potential.

meanings.short: The regime of strong enough accelerations in which MOND gives back Newton's law of gravity.
A choice of coordinates for a gravitational wave in which the metric change has no trace and lies across the direction of travel.
meanings.long: Only two components then remain, the two polarisations, called plus and cross. Their effect on a ring of free masses is to stretch it one way while squeezing it the other.

meanings.short: A measure of how stretched or squashed a distribution of mass or charge is, beyond its total amount and its lopsidedness.
meanings.long: For mass it is the integral of density times xᵢxⱼ. A changing mass quadrupole moment is the main source of gravitational waves, since mass and its dipole cannot oscillate.

meanings.short: The formula giving gravitational waves from a slowly moving source: their strength is set by the second time derivative of its quadrupole moment.
meanings.long: The wave amplitude is 2G/c⁴ times the second derivative of the moment divided by the distance. A related formula gives the power radiated, which explains the shrinking orbit of the Hulse–Taylor pulsar.

meanings.short: A tensor that removes the part of a vector or tensor along one direction, keeping only the part across it.
meanings.long: With n the direction of travel, Pᵢⱼ = δᵢⱼ − nᵢnⱼ. Applied to a gravitational wave, it picks out the part transverse to the wave.

meanings.short: A result linking the stresses inside a body to the second time derivative of its quadrupole moment, from conservation of energy and momentum.
meanings.long: It lets the gravitational waves of a source be written in terms of how its mass moves, which gives the quadrupole formula.

meanings.short: The effective stress-energy tensor of gravitational waves, averaged over several wavelengths, giving the energy and momentum they carry.
meanings.long: Energy of gravity cannot be pinned to a point, but averaged this way it is well defined. Richard Isaacson worked it out in 1968.

meanings.short: The rising frequency and strength of gravitational waves from two compact bodies spiralling together, like a bird's chirp turned into sound.
meanings.long: The waves carry off energy, so the orbit shrinks and speeds up. The way the frequency rises gives a combination of the two masses, the chirp mass.

everyday: Named after a bird's chirp, whose pitch also rises quickly.

meanings.short: A source of gravitational waves, such as merging neutron stars, whose signal gives its distance directly.
meanings.long: The shape of the waveform fixes how strong the waves were at the source, so their measured strength gives the distance, as a standard candle's brightness does.

meanings.short: An idealised body so small and light that it does not disturb the gravity around it, with no charge, size or spin.
meanings.long: A test body follows a geodesic. Real bodies with size feel tidal forces and drift off geodesics slightly.

meanings.short: The heavy mirrors of a gravitational-wave detector, hung so that they move freely and follow only the passing waves.
A small imagined object placed in a flow or field to show what it would do there, for example whether it would start to spin.
A space with the greatest possible number of symmetries, so that it looks the same at every point and in every direction.
meanings.long: In n dimensions it has n(n + 1)/2 Killing vectors. In three dimensions there are only three kinds: flat space, the sphere and the hyperbolic space, which are the space slices of FRW universes.

meanings.short: Short for Friedmann–Robertson–Walker: the standard model universe, uniform and the same in every direction, whose size changes with time.
meanings.long: Its metric is the Robertson–Walker metric, and the Friedmann equations give how its scale factor changes. Lemaître's name is often added, as FLRW.

meanings.short: The small difference in temperature of the cosmic microwave background between one side of the sky and the opposite side, caused by our own motion.
meanings.long: The Sun moves at about 370 km/s relative to the background, which makes it look about 0.1 per cent warmer ahead and cooler behind.

meanings.short: A bookkeeping term that writes the curvature of space in the Friedmann equation as if it were one more kind of density.
meanings.long: It falls as one over the scale factor squared. A closed universe has a negative curvature density, an open one a positive one.

meanings.short: An object of known true size, whose apparent size on the sky gives its distance.
meanings.long: The pattern of sound waves imprinted in the distribution of galaxies is the best-known cosmic standard ruler.

meanings.short: The distance worked out from an object's known size and the angle it covers on the sky.
meanings.long: In an expanding universe it is not the same as other distance measures: very distant objects can look larger again, because their light left when they were closer to us.

meanings.short: The distance worked out from an object's known sideways speed and how fast it appears to move across the sky.
meanings.long: In an expanding universe it equals the comoving distance in a flat universe, and links the other two measures: luminosity distance is (1 + z) times it, angular-diameter distance is it divided by (1 + z).

meanings.short: Setting distant clocks to agree by sending light signals back and forth and assuming light takes equal time each way.
meanings.long: It defines which events count as simultaneous for an observer. Observers moving relative to each other then disagree about simultaneity.

meanings.short: Of a tensor density: the power of the Jacobian determinant by which it differs from a true tensor when coordinates change.
meanings.long: The determinant of the metric has weight −2 and the Levi-Civita symbol weight 1; multiplying a density by a suitable power of the determinant's size makes a true tensor.

meanings.short: Of the universe or an era: with expansion driven mainly by radiation and very fast particles, as in the first tens of thousands of years.
meanings.long: Radiation's energy density falls as one over the scale factor to the fourth power, faster than matter's, so it dominated early and later gave way to matter. During this era the scale factor grows as the square root of time.

meanings.short: The pattern of which events in a spacetime can influence which others, set by the light cones.
meanings.long: Penrose diagrams are drawn to show it. Two spacetimes with the same causal structure agree about cause and effect even if their distances differ.

meanings.short: A way of combining two vector spaces into a larger one, whose members are sums of pairs, one from each space.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics the state space of two systems together is the tensor product of their separate spaces. If the spaces have dimensions m and n, the product has dimension m times n, and states that are not a single pair are entangled.

meanings.short: The part of a pattern or distribution that is stretched or squashed along an axis, the next detail after the total and the dipole.
meanings.long: A quadrupole pattern on the sky is brighter in two opposite directions and fainter in the two directions between them. Four charges at the corners of a square, alternating in sign, make an electric quadrupole.
